rv.q: At the start, the boyAlexander in his sailor suit steps forward and tells us with a touch of gleeful malice that we are about to see “the longest play in the history of the world”. On top of that, Ingmar Bergman’s Fanny &Alexander is all about a family of actors.
The overwhelming impression, though, is that this is feast of show.
It’s possessed of a surging emotional swoop and visual audacity that bursts its way into your heart.
I swung between enjoyment and bouts of thinking it was all becoming a touch pretentious, with references to Shakespeare and the theatre world pushing it dangerously close to a sort of self-reverence.
The evening gathers strength and inner life.
Yet this version by Stephen Beresford never quite convincingly makes the case for the transition from screen to stage.
This play has much going for it... But it is far too uneven.
This lush, haunting bedtime story unfolds in the sumptuous Old Vic as if it was written for it.
Translating a movie to the stage without reimagining the original in some way can be tricky. Adding songs to turn a film into a stage musical can often yield surprising results: The 2001.
There are some banal and even boring scenes which prevent the production from achieving greatness. But beautiful performances compensate for the occasional lacklustre sequences.
